analysis.one_liner: Replaces asbestos injury lawsuits with a federal compensation office and fund paid by defendant companies.
analysis.headline: The bill cleared the House Judiciary Committee on an 18-15 vote in July 2000, but the full House never voted on it before that Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would replace today's courtroom battles over asbestos injuries with a federal Office of Asbestos Compensation in the Justice Department. Every claimant with a qualifying asbestos-related illness would get a medical eligibility certificate, then mandatory settlement offers from each company named and an offer from a federal fund financed by assessments on defendants; claimants could still opt out and sue in court. The bill would largely eliminate punitive damages and screen out exposed workers who are not yet sick, while guaranteeing fast-tracked payments to workers who are. It was rewritten by the Republican-led House Judiciary Committee, reported 18-15, and never reached the floor.
analysis.who_benefits: Companies facing thousands of asbestos lawsuits would get a predictable administrative process, strict medical screening, and an end to most punitive damages. Genuinely sick workers would get guaranteed, fast-tracked settlement offers from a fund paid for by defendant assessments, reimbursement for medical testing, no time-bar defenses, and the right to come back later if a nonmalignant disease turns into cancer.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Asbestos defendants and seriously sick workers

how_it_helps.text: Every medically eligible claimant would get a mandatory good-faith settlement offer from each named defendant within 21 days, and an offer from the Asbestos Compensation Fund within 10 days after that, with enforceable deadlines on the government's own decisions.
Claimants who reject all offers may opt out and sue in any state or federal court, keeping a jury trial as a backstop.

No statute of limitations defense would be allowed unless the claim was already untimely at enactment, and a claim would not accrue until the worker's illness actually qualifies, ending dismissals of workers who file when they get sick.
A settlement or judgment for a non-malignant asbestos disease would not bar a later claim if the same person develops mesothelioma, lung cancer, or another qualifying cancer.
Heavily exposed workers would be reimbursed 100 percent of out-of-pocket costs for required medical testing, up to $1,500, with repeat testing every three years.
The new office would run a legal assistance program and claimants would keep the right to hire any lawyer they choose, though fees would be subject to reasonableness rules.

analysis.who_pays: Claimants with the strongest cases would give up the most: punitive damages would be nearly eliminated, available only on clear and convincing evidence of flagrant indifference and capped at three times the award, and damages for enhanced risk of future disease would be excluded except in limited cases. Exposed workers who are not yet impaired would get nothing beyond testing reimbursement. Taxpayers would fund the new office, with first-year appropriations capped at $250 million.
analysis.who_pays_short: Victims with strong cases and taxpayers

drawbacks.text: Punitive damages would be available only if the claimant proves by clear and convincing evidence that a defendant acted with conscious, flagrant indifference to safety, and they would be capped at three times the compensatory award.
Damages solely for enhanced risk of a future condition would be excluded, so exposed-but-healthy workers could not recover for the risk hanging over them, only medical testing reimbursement.

Compensation would require meeting strict medical eligibility criteria — specific x-ray findings, breathing-test thresholds, and exposure history — so workers exposed to asbestos without a qualifying impairment would be screened out of compensation.
The scheme would be financed partly by federal appropriations, up to $250 million in the first year and $150 million in later years, a public cost on top of the defendant assessments.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: This was a negotiated trade, not a one-sided giveaway. Sick workers would get something the current system often fails to deliver — guaranteed offers within weeks rather than years of litigation that many die before finishing — plus fixes for real abuses like time-bar defenses and settlements that block later cancer claims. The cost falls on the claimants with the strongest cases, who would lose punitive damages and enhanced-risk claims, and on workers not yet sick. The committee's narrow 18-15 report shows even its own members did not agree on whether that trade was sensible tort reform or an industry liability cap; the full House never got to say.

outcome.mechanism: The committee reported the bill to the House's floor calendar on July 24, 2000, but House leaders never brought it up for a vote before the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001.

narrative.text: Henry Hyde, chairman of the House Judiciary Committee, introduced the bill on March 25, 1999 with a bipartisan group of original co-sponsors including Democrat James Moran of Virginia.
The bill was referred to the Judiciary Committee, which held hearings on July 1, 1999 and marked it up in March 2000.

The committee rewrote the bill from the 1999 version — which would have barred most asbestos lawsuits outright and barred class actions without defendant consent — into a version with an opt-out right to sue, a legal assistance program, limited punitive damages, and penalties for lowball settlement offers.
On March 16, 2000 the committee ordered the amended bill reported by a vote of 18 to 15.
The bill was reported amended on July 24, 2000 as H. Rept. 106-782 and placed on the Union Calendar, Calendar No. 449, where it stayed; no floor vote ever followed.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, asbestos victims kept the existing court system, including full punitive damages and jury trials, and the plaintiff-side trial bar kept its litigation practice. The defendant companies that had pushed for a national liability cap got nothing, and sick workers kept waiting years for court awards.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Victims and trial lawyers; defendants got no relief

for.name: Henry Hyde
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill, held committee hearings, and steered the rewritten version out of committee on an 18-15 vote on July 24, 2000.

for.name: James Moran
for.what_they_did: Joined Hyde as an original co-sponsor when the bill was introduced.

for.name: Asbestos defendant companies and insurers
for.what_they_did: Publicly pushed for a national administrative settlement scheme to replace asbestos jury trials.

against.name: House Republican floor leadership
against.role: House leadership controlling the floor calendar
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a floor vote after it was placed on the Union Calendar in July 2000.

against.name: 15 House Judiciary Committee members
against.role: Committee members voting no in markup
against.what_they_did: Voted against ordering the bill reported on March 16, 2000, leaving the 18-15 margin.

against.name: Association of Trial Lawyers of America
against.what_they_did: Campaigned against restructuring asbestos litigation out of the courts.

against.name: AFL-CIO and industrial unions
against.what_they_did: Opposed early versions of the bill as inadequate for exposed and sick workers.

sides.party_line_note: Of the bill's 77 cosponsors, 71 were Republicans and 6 were Democrats, and the Judiciary Committee reported it on a narrow 18-15 vote; the bill never reached the House floor, where its fate would have been decided.

industries.industry: Asbestos product manufacturers and other corporate defendants
industries.note: The bill would replace jury trials with a mandatory administrative settlement process, screen out claims by exposed-but-unimpaired people, and mostly eliminate punitive damages, sharply cutting defendants' costs. In exchange, defendants would pay assessments financing a guaranteed federal fund offer to every medically eligible claimant.
A predictable, administratively capped claims process would reduce the open-ended long-tail asbestos exposure on insurers' books, though they would share the assessment burden financing the fund.
The administrative process, mandatory settlement offers, and federal fee-reasonableness rules would shrink the contingency-fee litigation practice built on asbestos jury cases.
The bill leaves existing court-supervised asbestos trusts untouched unless they elect to join the new scheme, locking in their existing role paying victims.
